item.title: Just How Rosy Is That Datacenter Buildout Forecast?
item.description:
No matter how much money anyone throws at it, the GenAI boom can only continue to grow as fast as datacenters are built and powered up to accept machinery.

No amount of political, social, or economic pressure can speed up how power generation equipment is installed at datacenters or at utilities. No one was expecting this AI boom to skyrocket so, and supply chains from chip manufacturing equipment to chip makers to those who make all of the equipment that goes into power distribution in the electric grids and within the datacenters were not ready to ramp as quickly as the industry seems to require.

For now at least, it takes people to build all of these datacenters and indeed anything else we want to provide shelter for ourselves, our businesses, and our public facilities. And it is convenient, perhaps, that there are high interest rates for mortgages at a time when datacenter builders want more people working on their projects instead of building homes or offices. (Yes, people still go to the office, and thankfully I have not had to do that since 1996.)

Jason Furman , an economics professor at Harvard University, posted this neat chart on X that shows the growth rates of construction projects thus far in 2026 up through August:

This is yet another data point that shows just how much datacenter construction and power utility construction are helping to prop up the economy in the United States. And just to be clear, this data from the US Census Bureau and the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, and it includes the cost of construction materials and the labor on construction projects. It explicitly does not include any compute, storage, or networking gear inside of those datacenters, but it does include the cost of power distribution and energy backup equipment in datacenter facilities.

As you can see, datacenter capacity construction increases, and to a certain extent for power utilities as well, are counter-balancing the declines seen in commercial and residential construction in the United States.

It is tough to get a sense of the spending levels for datacenters from this chart, and so we poked around and found a monthly chart that runs from January 2014 through August 2026 from the US Census Bureau, which was put together by the Our World In Data project at Oxford University. Take a look:

This chart is based on inflation-adjusted spending pegged to 2021 US dollars.

You can really see how the GenAI boom, which is driving datacenter construction spending increases in the United States, started in November 2022. Since that time, we are in a very different market – up and to the right, and accelerating.

This data from the Census Bureau does not include datacenter spending by federal, state, or local governments, buy the way. Not that this is very large compared to what the hyperscalers, cloud builders, and AI model builders are ponying up. Government datacenter spending would be a tiny part of the signal that would not change its shape by much.

Which brings me to a very detailed and interesting forecast of datacenter spending that the analysts at Jeffries put together with the help of Aterio , a market researcher specialized in datacenter forecasts among many other sectors.

Aterio provided the historical context, and Jonathan Petersen, managing director at Jeffries, put together a base forecast with a bull and a bear variant to that base case to bracket what they expect datacenter spending to be from 2026 through 2030. Here’s the table that gives you the data:

And for those of you who also like to look at data visually, here is the companion chart:

Our thanks to Petersen for permission to share this data with you.

“The AI industry has a datacenter problem,” Petersen writes in a report released on October 9. “Demand for inference and frontier model training is growing faster than developers can bring capacity online. Our dataset tracks ~65 IT GW of DCs under construction (~140 percent of installed capacity), and another ~361 GW of future announced projects (~760 percent). However, it will take time to bring that capacity online, and many projects will be delayed or canceled. We expect 12.9 GWs of new capacity in 2026 and 18 GWs in 2027.”

This model only predicts installed gigawatts in North America for IT gear, not the cost of building those datacenters or putting the gear inside them to make them useful or the power and cooling costs that enliven the facilities and gear. This model does not just take the forecasts by datacenter operators and businesses that run their own datacenters at face value, but looks at the probability that projects will be completed, and to what extend based on intentions.

To say the least, Jeffries is appropriately cynical about how the datacenter buildout will pan out, given the constraints on all of the supply inputs and labor to build datacenters.

“The ability to bring new datacenter capacity online is often reduced to a discussion measuring new grid interconnects or behind-the-meter power generation as primary gating factors,” says Petersen. “Or tracking hyperscaler capex and assuming that spending more capex will create new data centers. Or, measuring chip sales projections from the semiconductor industry. But any of those discussions in isolation misses the bigger picture: it takes all of those inputs, plus available labor, manufacturing of electrical and cooling equipment, and a cooperative political and regulatory environment to move a data center project from the pipeline to online capacity.”

The labor shortage and the increasing political pressure for datacenters to pay their fair share of the cost of electricity generation and a rising skepticism about the financial benefits to the communities that host datacenters is what is driving the bear case. The bull case is more about supply chain issues for datacenter construction easing somewhat, but not enough for everything desired and planned to be built. This latter point is the point . Even the bull case assumes lots of delays and some cancellations.

To show you the gap between planned capacity and the estimates by Jeffries, even the hyperscalers, who have tons of money and very strong balance sheets, are not going to be able to build at the rate they want. The planned and estimated North American hyperscaler datacenter capacity for 2026 is 6.21 gigawatts in 2026. (The year is pretty much done, so this convergence makes sense.) For 2027, the hyperscalers in North America are talking about wanting to do 8.37 gigawatts of datacenter buildout, but Jeffries thinks only 7.53 gigawatts will get built for these companies. In 2028, the aspirations are huge, and the built capacity Jeffries expects will be lower, not higher, with hyperscalers planning for 10.13 gigawatts of buildout and Petersen and crew expecting only 6.54 gigawatts to be completed. The 2029 plans are for just under 18 gigawatts among the hyperscalers in North America, but Jeffries thinks only 5.86 gigawatts will get done. And in 2030, the aspirations will shrink to 13.82 gigawatts for the hyperscaler facilities in the United States and Canada and the expected build will look more like 4.46 gigawatts.

These are huge gaps. In 2026, labor is the biggest damper on datacenter spending, and in 2027 through 2029, it will be cooling equipment. In 2030, the main constraint will be available power, says Jeffries. All of these constraints are always present, of course.

item.title: PARTNER CONTENT: When Faster Supercomputers Aren’t Enough
item.description:
When a million veterans shared their genetic data by enrolling in the Department of Veterans Affairs' “Million Veteran Program,” they expected nothing back. This did not surprise Ravi Madduri, a senior scientist with the Data Science and Learning Division at the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Argonne National Laboratory. He is abundantly clear about the terms under which these veterans donated their data: “Even after giving everything to the country, they found it in their hearts to give more without expecting anything in return.”

That gift, which constituted the nation’s largest biorepository and most ancestrally varied cohorts of veteran data in the world, created a debt that Madduri, who also holds a joint appointment in the Department of Human Genetics at the University of Chicago, is working to repay.

“What I feel when I look at that data is that I have an obligation to deliver to the veterans on their intentions in doing this,” he says. Those intentions, as he reads it, are that others, veteran or not, can benefit from whatever the data can reveal.

“We cannot dilly dally,” Madduri says.

After arriving at Argonne as a graduate student in 2001, Madduri has spent the last two decades at the intersection of supercomputing and biomedicine, much of the time building the computing that turns the veterans’ data into results impacting areas from post-traumatic stress disorder to heart disease to cancer.

He explains that machines have largely held up their end, but the obstacles between precious data and delivered results are not always solved with faster machines. Understanding the challenges is the path toward better science.

What The Math Was Unable To Solve

Any two human genomes differ at millions of specific positions. A genome-wide association study asks a seemingly simple question across an enormous volume of data. For example, does a given genetic variant travel together with a particular medical condition ? On its own, the question is simple. Multiplied across every variant worth testing and every condition recorded in a patient's chart, it becomes an enormous math problem, which is what supercomputers exist to solve. The harder question is whether the code is written to let them.

Madduri's team has run this problem on the Summit system at DOE's Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility and on the Aurora system at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility. On Summit, the team found that the job would not finish on the machine's CPUs. As the cohort grew, the matrix the analysis needed for each group no longer fit in memory, and the job stalled.

“We decided to open the box and look at the code,” Madduri said. They found that the issue was not merely a speed problem, but a coding one.

The analysis had been written for ordinary processors because that is what the genetics community was running on. Underneath the algorithms, though, the code spent nearly all of its time doing one thing: multiplying very large grids of numbers. This is exactly the operation that graphics processors exist to perform, and what makes them the engine of modern artificial intelligence training. As Madduri notes, the same computational architecture accelerating AI discovery “is also foundational for population genomics.” So, the team, led on this effort by Argonne's Alex Rodriguez, rewrote that part of the code for GPUs, and an analysis that would have taken roughly 481,000 CPU-core hours in the original version became tractable. This shift did more than speed up a slow job. It made a virtually impossible job possible.

The workhorse they accelerated is a widely used genetics package called SAIGE, which made the rewritten version SAIGE-GPU , described in a separate paper in Bioinformatics.

"We are not good at coming up with names. Sorry," Madduri says sheepishly.

Before SAIGE-GPU, nearly every genome-wide association study started by picking a disease then looking for the variants linked to it. Madduri is blunt about the cost of that approach.

“One of the challenges I found in biomedical research is that it is very incremental,” he explains. “Every year, they get new datasets, they analyze the data, they find a new set of genetic variants, and this happens across all of the different diseases.” The reason, he adds, is limited access to large-scale computing.

His team chose not to be incremental and decided to solve the computational challenge once and for all.

“One of the challenges we set for ourselves was to just take all the data that we have available, all the genetic data for all the veterans that have been sequenced as part of the Million Veteran Program,” Madduri says.

The team, the Million Veteran Program consortium, published the results in Science , with Madduri's group among the authors, and published the computational work separately in Bioinformatics. The study reported on 2,068 traits across 635,969 veterans, and the results flagged 13,672 regions of the genome linked to one or more conditions. About 1,600 of these regions surfaced only because nearly a third of the participants were not of European ancestry. According to the Science paper, most genetic studies to this point have been drawn overwhelmingly from people of European descent. These 1,600 associations were previously “invisible” in the populations studied.

That ancestral range also shaped how the analysis had to be run. The groups could not simply be pooled. That is, if a condition is more common in one ancestral group than another, the analysis has no way to tell a genuine disease marker from a marker of simply belonging to that group. Each group had to be run separately, and the results combined afterward. The 1,600 associations exist in no single group's results. They appear only when the separate analyses are combined.

Madduri is careful about what the whole exercise means and what it does not.

“This is all preclinical,” he says. “This is the discovery phase.” The analysis produces a statistical map of where to look. Turning any one of those 13,672 regions into a treatment takes years of downstream work by researchers who pick up and follow the data, which is why Madduri says the team never stopped.

“Things that took 14 days when we wrote the Science paper now take less than a couple of hours,” he says. While this means getting an answer sooner, the real win is being able to ask the same question of a bigger population “with a larger cohort size and more statistical rigor than the paper that we published a couple of years ago.”

When Data Cannot Travel

The veterans’ genomes have an unusual advantage over other medical data. One agency gathered the data under one agreement, which is what made bringing them to Summit possible. In medicine, Madduri says, data “cannot be shared with one another as freely as you would probably share cosmology data.”

The alternative is to move the model, he says: “Federated learning allows you to train models without moving data around.” This means each institution trains on the copy it already holds, behind its own walls, and only sends back the adjustments the model learned. Those adjustments are combined into a single updated model, which goes out to everyone, and the cycle repeats.

Asked how several institutions are persuaded to compute together without pooling anything, he corrects the premise. “It is not the institution,” he says. “The first layer of that puzzle is people wanting to work together, to collaborate.” Then, the part that makes it work: “It is a people federation.”

Madduri was a co-developer of APPFL, the Argonne Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning framework, which provides a means to help “move” models rather than data. The machinery underneath is closer to access control than to machine learning.

"You do not have to write code for each scheduler," he says. Globus Compute presents one interface across the facilities' schedulers, and APPFL submits its training jobs through it.

Even with these technical challenges, the harder problem is permission.

“All the computing that happens is authorized computing that is tied to a project allocation,” Madduri says. Federated training means that each collaborator’s job has to run under their own institutional credentials on a machine they are personally entitled to use. A site with data nobody else has makes that shared model better for everyone.

"If one site has data that are unique to it and other sites do not have that, then the model becomes more robust," Madduri adds.

Many Different Worlds

Madduri has been a regular attendee at the SC Conference since SC01 in Denver, which was themed “Beyond Boundaries,” and focused on moving data across them.

“I was a grad student, and I had a demo in the DOE booth demonstrating my master’s thesis, which at that time was to use the Internet to move large amounts of data reliably from one point to the other,” he says. That capability was called reliable file transfer, and, in his words, it “has now transformed into what is called ‘Globus’.” The first tool he helped build moved research data around. The latest one lets the data stay in place.

Since SC01, Madduri has been to the conference roughly 20 times and is specific about what he takes home.

“I learn parallel processing, how people are scaling AI training, how people are dealing with parallelization, how people are dealing with resource utilization monitoring,” he notes. His group attends the Computational Approaches for Cancer Workshop every year. Lately, the interest has moved to AI agents.

“The agentic approaches are the next frontier for us,” he declares.

Madduri is also aware that he walks in unusual research domains. Before biomedicine, he worked with high-energy physicists, earthquake engineers, and cosmologists.

“When I go to SC, I live in many different worlds,” he says. “I am part of a very small group of people that go to a [combined] human genetics conference and a supercomputing conference.”

For Madduri, his debt is not settled. More than a decade after the first veterans enrolled, the Million Veteran Program data have produced a map but not yet a cure. What stands between those two things is the work of getting separate institutions to compute as one. To date, that still is being done largely by hand.

“For the earlier experiments, it was us talking to NERSC, us talking to Argonne, us talking to Oak Ridge,” Madduri says. “It is a lot of human in the loop.” He is hoping the American Science Cloud being built under the DOE’s Genesis Mission will take that over: “It would be automated, run using APIs.”

For now, Madduri remains focused on turning data into triumph, using a very special cohort of data to reveal the next breakthrough against cancer or spare someone a lifetime of anxiety. Until then, he marks progress one good idea, one technical advancement, and one SC Conference at a time.

“My connection to Supercomputing, to SC, is long and very fruitful,” Madduri says. “I will be back in November, in Chicago, for SC26.”

Join the Conversation at SC26

SC26 brings together the people building the computing infrastructure the work described herein depends on: systems, data platforms, networks, and storage that let research run at scale and across institutions.

Attendees engage with technical papers, workshops, tutorials, posters, and Birds of a Feather (BoF) sessions covering AI, quantum computing, and HPC alongside practitioners from national laboratories, industry, and academia working on similar problems. Madduri will also be part of the SC26 Regional Tech Hub , a multimedia forum making its conference debut in Chicago, where he will contribute to the High-throughput Computing Infrastructures and Systems area.

Join us in Chicago, November 15–20, 2026, for a week of discovery, collaboration, and community with a spotlight on regional technology leaders. Register today!

item.title: A Decade In, zeroRISC Sees A Bright Future For Open Silicon
item.description:
At the Hot Chips conference in 2018, Google hardware engineers detailed their recently introduced “Titan” chip , which was designed to create a silicon root of trust (RoT) in servers. RoT is part of a larger push by processor designers at the time to ensure security in the wake of the Spectre and Meltdown vulnerabilities. They also talked about plans to make it available as an open source offering, another step in the nascent open-silicon movement.

Leading the charge on OpenTitan for Google at the time was Dominic Rizzo, who pushed the effort and served as its technical lead manager for five years.

“The way I sold OpenTitan inside Google was they were buying a lot of heterogenous hardware for the cloud and it made their security posture a little lumpy,” Rizzo tells The Next Platform . “OpenTitan was really the first truly credible, well-resourced, do-it-right-from-scratch open source silicon project.”

For Rizzo, it was the starting point for what has become decade-long effort to push the open silicon rock up the hill. He left Google in 2023 but continues to be the project director for OpenTitan for lowRISC, the official maintainer and host of OpenTitan. The same year he departed Google, Rizzo co-founded and is now the CEO of zeroRISC, a startup aimed at pushing for broad commercial adoption of open silicon RoT.

In May, zeroRISC – along with other industry players, including Qualcomm, Analog Devices, and Meta, and the Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy – launched Pavona under the auspices of GlobalPlatform, a nonprofit standards consortium. Pavona – which Rizzo chairs – is a neutral ecosystem for designing open and secure hardware, similar to how the open source Yocto Project and Zephyr Project work for software. Pavona includes a production-stage post-quantum cryptography (PQC) stack that supports various algorithms, including ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA, and a composable platform organization can use to build hardware RoTs and chip subsystems.

The arguments for open silicon essentially dovetail with those for open source software, he says. Those include reducing costs by eliminating licensing fees and royalties that come with commercial chips from the likes of Intel, AMD, and Nvidia, reusing infrastructure, and providing better collaboration. Innovation can be faster, greater transparency and trust throughout the supply chain, and having more people involved in the design, which can mean more eyes to detect and fix vulnerabilities and defects.

The idea of open source silicon rose about the same time as open source software and Linux became a thing, Rizzo says. It just couldn’t get momentum behind it.

“It has a lot to do with inconsistent interfaces, inconsistent standards, the fact that roles for engineers in the silicon industry are very specific,” he says. “There's a backend production person, there's a layout person, there's an analog person, there's a digital designer, there is a DV person. It's not like software. There is not really that kind of movement within those roles. They get very, very specialized, so this notion of 'there's this open project that does all these things, leverage it how you will,' that never really took off. There's also a lot fewer people who do it than do software.”

However, evolution in the semiconductor industry have helped fuel the recent expansion, including the adoption of the IP business model, according to lowRISC.

“All chip designs today are modular, and the vast majority adopt third-party IP from IP vendors like Arm and Synopsys, and foundries like TSMC,” the company wrote earlier this year. “This IP reuse has brought to the industry a major reduction in development cost and time and increase in quality, which are benefits typically associated with open source. ... It is only a small step for silicon vendors to start using open-source IP instead of that from commercial vendors.”

In addition, the open RISC-V architecture continues to mature since it’s introduction in 2010 and is broadly adopted in embedded systems, with a push being made to carry it over into the datacenter .

“RISC-V almost gave permission because RISC-V is an open source instruction set architecture,” Rizzo says. “Even before, when those things were all super proprietary, Arm famously made quite a bit of money off proprietary ISAs, but what that did is ask the natural question: If you've got an open source ISA, why not open source implementation? That's a natural next step. That granting of permission helped a lot as well.”

In addition, lowRISC’s Ibex CPU (below) was released in 2019 and is now in various SoC designs.

In 2014, Nuvoton in 2024 brought to market a discrete RoT security chip (below) based on OpenTitan and announced Google’s plans to use it in Chromebooks running ChromeOS.

In 2025 came the first release Caliptra (below), RoT architecture that includes OpenTitan elements. It was developed through the CHIPS Alliance and Open Compute Project by such vendors as Microsoft, Google, AMD, and Nvidia, and is designed for datacenter-level SoCs.

Over the past few years, the industry has begun to see more companies and industry groups enter it. lowRISC was launched in 2014, and SiFive – which offers custom silicon solutions based on RISC-V – emerged from stealth two years later . The Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions Alliance , or CHERI, was founded in 2024 with a membership that includes Arm, Google, the UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), and, lowRISC. The technology, which aims to protect data stored in hardware memory by building security into hardware.

zeroRISC also focuses on security with what it calls its “silicon trust stack.” The company’s offerings include a Pavona repository and collaboration layer for chip design teams, with version control, review workflows, and build artifacts, continuous integration that includes verification workloads for physical hardware, and post quantum-ready silicon IP. There’s also a provisioning service that includes a line-side server for the datacenter that is backed by a hardware security module (HSM) and management service that offers OEM debugging and over-the-air updates.

In May, the company unveiled the open source release of its cryptographic hardware and software stack for both classical and post-quantum environments. It includes a configurable Cryptolib embedded library in its silicon platform that has a programmable asymmetric cryptography coprocessor (ACC) for post-quantum and classical asymmetric algorithms and dedicated hardware accelerators for symmetric operations like AES and SHA2/3.

PQC is a key challenge for the industry and organizations like Pavona, according to Rizzo. The U.S. government and its counterparts in Europe and elsewhere are setting aggressive deadlines for organizations to institute such technologies to address the upcoming quantum computing era. Quantum systems are expected to be able to quickly decrypt data that is protected by AES-256 and similar encrypting techniques, and that threat groups with access to such computers will be able to access data they may have already stolen but can yet access, a threat called “harvest now, decrypt later.”

Google has placed that time as early as 2029, while others are looking at 2030 or later. Moving to PQC is a significant transition for companies, the type that only comes once in a lifetime or so, and it’s beginning to happen with ML-DSA, MLKEM, and SPHINCS+, with more on the way, Rizzo says.

“PQ cryptography, it's a bit more of a pain to implement than the classical cryptography because in classical cryptographic, you have one hard problem that tends to be at the root of all of these pictographic operations and primitives, especially for asymmetric” cryptography, he says. “Post-quantum cryptography does not work the same way and the trade-offs are a lot more varied and the underlying hard problems are different, and then the implementations for the different operations are themselves also different.”

Going forward, there are things that need to be address, he says. With Pavona, IP work, like with block design and development, is being done, but a lot of the effort is going into areas like infrastructure, configurability and flexibility that will make it easier for organizations to use open silicon technologies. Governance also is a key issue.

“That’s one of the more interesting aspects of this whole thing because we can build the technology in the open,” Rizzo says. “We understand how to do that. It's more like, how do you sustain it for the long term? How do you build the real ecosystem around it? How do you make it so that everyone benefits to some degree, not just a single supporter?”

In addition, new regulations like the European Union’s Cyber Resilience Act are shifting the liability for cyber incidents onto the device makers, which is forcing them to look at what they implement and what they take responsibility for, and to dig deeper into their supply chains to ensure they have greater control over what they’re building, he says.

“You need to have a hardware root of trust below the software that you can reset back to a known good state or all hope is lost,” Rizzo says. “That’s dawning on people. You need to actually have control over the chips. The software attack surface has always been large, but now the attack capability has grown to match that large surface. The way you address that is you have a silicon root of trust.”

item.title: Cisco Turns Its Attention To The Control Layers Of Its Quantum Network
item.description:
Cisco Networks, through its Outshift R&D and incubator unit, has for several years been piecing together the network architecture needed for quantum computing. The company believes that scaling quantum environments will not only mean creating larger systems to handle the massive numbers of qubits that will run applications. Scaling also will require connecting quantum computers through networks to create distributed and cloud-like architectures, similar to their classical computing counterparts.

In short, it is about scaling out rather than simply scaling up.

Early last year, the Outshift group was put in charge of building the quantum networking stack (below) and later in 2025 unveiled the prototype of its quantum network entangling chip , which works by generating entangled pairs of photons over large distances. Such entanglement can’t be done with classical bits of information, and is a key part of what makes quantum systems so much faster and more powerful.

In April, Cisco introduced the working prototype of its Universal Quantum Switch, which is designed to connect quantum sensors and quantum systems not only created by different vendors but also that use different modalities, such as superconducting , photonics , neutral atoms , and trapped ions .

Now Cisco is pulling in the tools needed to scale the quantum network itself. At the Cisco’s Quantum Summit this month, the company announced the Quantum Network Controller , another research prototype that provides the control layer needed replace the manual work being done now with automation that can keep up with machine speed of the any-to-any connections that the Universal Quantum Switch enables.

“Connecting 1,000 quantum nodes point to point takes close to 500,000 dedicated links,” wrote Vijoy Pandey, senior vice president of Outshift.

The problem, according to Ramana Kompella, head of Cisco Research, is that right now, in these relatively early days of quantum development, much of the work is still being done by humans. That won’t last as demand on the networks scale.

“Where we are today, if you look at the quantum networks, they're very point-to-point, manually stitched together and configured,” Kompella tells The Next Platform . “The moment you actually have application scale requests coming in at machine speeds, essentially saying, ‘I want to be able to entangle this node and this node,’ that's the power of a network. Any nodes would want to properly exchange entanglements, so if you have these requests coming in at machine speeds, the human way of configuring and reconfiguring the fabric is not going to scale. That's why you need a control plane that can scale and operate at machine speeds, which is where the controller comes into play.”

Classical systems already use controllers to automate operations and manage resources, expose APIs, and other actions, but they’re deterministic – their execution timing, task scheduling, and other steps are predictable and repeatable. Quantum is a different and more complex animal, says Reza Nejabati, head of quantum research and Quantum Labs at Cisco. It’s probabilistic, with qubits that have short-lived coherence times, with various factors like loss, fidelity, synchronization and the performance of the system determining the success or failure of an operation. Cisco is aiming to shield application developers from quantum’s complexity, Nejabati  says.

Cisco’s controller does this by acting as an abstraction layer, providing what Pandey called an Entanglement-as-a-Service model, exposing an API for everything from switches to detectors to timing systems. An application can request entanglement by pointing to the endpoints fidelity, rate, fidelity, and timing it needs, and the controller schedules the connection to address the demand. It goes on to ensure the quality of the link, uses predefined tuning, and if performance falters, retries or reinitializes the job.

The controller also allows quantum systems – and their various modalities – to hook into the network. For Cisco, like IBM and others, the modality of choice is superconducting.

“ We would love to think that everything will be built by Cisco, but the reality is we will work with many different components coming in from many different vendors,” Kompella says. “It's also the goal of this to try and hide the complexity associated with onboarding many different types of devices and shield all this complexity to the applications. That's really the missing piece without which you cannot actually scalably operate your quantum networks in the future.”

Another step for Cisco is its Network-Aware Quantum Compiler . Organizations need applications to be able to integrate and talk with the controller (below).

“ The first application that we tackle is the distributed quantum computing compiler, which effectively takes a large circuit, breaks it up into smaller pieces, and drives the network with the help of this controller in distributing entanglements at the right time so that your partial computed state is actually moving from processor A to processor B,” Kompella says. “Together, these are the missing pieces.”

Pandey sees the controller and compiler working together. The compiler works out the computation the application needs – how much entanglement the network needs to provide, the nodes involved, and the fidelity needed. From there, the controller puts all of that onto the network.

The quantum networking space is getting a growing amount of attention, with some estimates of the market’s size are in the range of $2 billion and vendors including Nu Quantum, Photonics Inc., Aliro Technologies, and QphoX. There also is Qunnect, which Cisco partnered with earlier this year in a demonstration of quantum scaling entanglement swapping on 17.6 kilometers New York City’s telecom fiber network.

Kompella notes that quantum use cases aren’t the only ones that can benefit from quantum networking. There also are classical computing applications that can be helped now. One example is decision coordination, a high-speed trading application in the financial services industry that can use a tool like Cisco’s Quantum Sync for instant communication between geographically separated nodes.

A quantum eavesdropper detection application uses quantum signals, mixing in quantum-entangled photons with classical photons on the same optical fiber, he says, adding that “if there is an eavesdropper in the middle, they're basically disturbing the entanglements. As a result, you can detect them.”

The development of quantum networks is still in the early phases, but Kompella says that interconnected quantum systems could on the scene in three to five years. However, still much needs to be done. One hurdle that needs to be cleared involves transduction, the conversion of quantum signals and information from one physical domain or frequency to another while preserving superposition, entanglement and other quantum properties. Or as Kompella puts it, “where your computational qubits meet the communication qubits.”

Another is quantum memory, or the storing of data as qubits. The challenge is the fragility of qubits, which can be easily disrupted and lose their quantum properties by light, vibrations, or other noises.

“Quantum memories are actually extremely helpful in increasing your fidelities and timing and coordinating between many different quantum nodes,” he says. “That's an area where quantum memories is still nascent and you probably need to see some more advances in realizing some of these cutting-edge applications.”

item.title: Microsoft’s “Clea” Maia 300 Inference XPU Is A Bandwidth Beast
item.description:
If everyone has an AI inference problem, with tokens still being too expensive to generate even with state of the art GPU and XPU accelerators, Microsoft probably has the biggest inference problem in the world.

For one thing, running inference for OpenAI ChatGPT models as well as helping the AI model builder  train its models is a big job. And then all of Microsoft’s worker productivity and back office applications are being infused with AI routines, and this is driving usage up the hockey stick handle at a rapid pace.

That is why Microsoft is putting the pedal to the metal with its Maia family of custom, homegrown XPU accelerators, and letting customers know Microsoft is working on the problem is why the company has rolled out the feeds and speeds on its future “Clea” Maia 300 accelerator as the Open Compute Project Summit 2026 kicks off this week.

The Maia 300 chip is a much-improved device, and it has a number of architectural changes that are designed to allow GenAI inference to run not only faster, but to scale up further so that larger agentic workloads, that consist of dozens to hundreds of models – implicitly through a mixture of experts foundation model, actually physically distinct independent models, or a mix of the two – working in concert and needing to share the same network and memory space to work efficiently and with low latency.

Microsoft is no slouch when it comes to designing chips, and it often gets things right on the second or third try. The software and cloud giant dipped its toe in the water with the “Athena” Maia 100 XPU in November 2023 . At the time, Microsoft was also unveiling its Cobalt 100 custom Arm server CPU, and it said very little about the architecture of either custom chip.

The second generation “Braga” Maia 200, which was only unveiled in January of this year , is a much more serious XPU and is the one that has been ramping into production on the Azure cloud this year.

In a separate announcement by Scott Guthrie , executive vice president in charge of Cloud and AI at Microsoft, he said that the “multigenerational Azure Maia program has become a foundational element of Microsoft’s AI infrastructure strategy,” and said that Maia 200 chips are doing inference for Copilot, helping the Microsoft AI team to develop new models, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry shifting to Maia 200s by the end of the year. (GitHub Copilot was supported by Maia 100s previously.) The Maia 200s will run OpenAI’s various models, Microsoft’s own models, and various open source models through Microsoft Foundry. It is not clear how much of OpenAI’s GPT API service is running on Maia 100 or Maia 200 iron.

The rumor mill is that Microsoft wants to get at least 1 million Maia sockets into the field, and Guthrie said in his statement that Maia would have “multi-gigawatt deployments” on the Azure cloud. A gigawatt of Maia 300s is around 575,000 devices, all in at 1.74 kilowatts for each accelerator and its portion of the system host, storage, and scale up networking. (Microsoft said a rack of Maia 300s burned about 167 kilowatts and has 96 XPUs interlinked.)

This Braga chip had much more HBM memory capacity and bandwidth even as it trimmed back on the on-chip SRAM cache. Moreover, it sported a much improved AI Transport Layer (ATL) custom RoCE Ethernet implementation that sported 2.3X more bandwidth while scaling up the cluster coherence domain of Maia cluster by 2.7X to 6,144 devices while only increasing power consumption by 1.5X. By shifting from 6-bit MX6 data formats to 4-bit MXFP4 and boosting the number of compute cores by 1.5X while at the same time boosting the clock speed, the Braga chip had 3.4X more floating point oomph than the Athena chip it replaced.

The Clea Maia 300 chip – really a chip complex in a socket, perhaps a system in a socket and not, strictly speaking, a system on a chip as Microsoft refers to it in its technical deep dive since it is actually a collection of seven chips and eight HBM stacks on an interposer – is pushing the envelope on all spec fronts, but is clearly focused on effective performance on real-world GenAI inference workloads and not on just cramming flops in a socket for speeds and feeds spec sheet superiority. Moreover, Microsoft has changed its ATL Ethernet network so it can cram more XPUs into a rack and more racks into a coherent domain to take on bigger agentic workflows.

The Maia 300 “system in socket” and the racks of machines to make up pod and superpod clusters have a hierarchy of compute, memory, and networking to glue together aggregations of these capacities to bring them to bear on GenAI work.

The Clea compute tiles are a little different from the ones comprising its Athena and Braga predecessors. All three XPUs have cores with a tile tensor unit (TTU) and a tile vector processor (TVP) as week as a tile data movement engine (TDMA) and tile control processor (TCP), plus L1 SRAM cache memory for these units to share. (How much was not divulged.) The Athena XPU organized four of these cores on a tile and sixteen tiles into a cluster (an in-socket cluster, that is) to get 64 cores in total. The organization of the Braga tiles and tile clusters was not divulged last January, but a paper was published on arXiv back in August that did and that has allowed us to update our salient characteristics monster table for the Maia lineup.

The Braga XPU, as it turns out, has tensor units with matrices that are twice as large as the Athena unit, so it took a little less than half as many cores to get the throughput Microsoft pegged for the device than we thought back in January’s story. The Braga XPU has ten tiles per on-chip cluster and four clusters for a total of 40 cores. They run at 2 GHz, and only nine cores are active per cluster to produce yield on the 3 nanometer N3P process used to etch the chip by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. The Athena and Braga chips were monolithic designs, and close to the reticle limit of lithography machines.

With the Clea XPU, Microsoft is moving to the 2 nanometer N2P process from TSMC and is also moving to a chiplet architecture that breaks out I/O and HBM controllers separate from the compute and SRAM cache elements. With Maia 300, there are four tile clusters, just like with the Maia 200, but each on-chip cluster has twelve tiles. There are also two elements, a reshaper and a tile synchronizer, that were added to the architecture with the Maia 200, but which we did not know about earlier this year, that help with the dataflow that spans the entire system, from the network down to the server node and all the way down to the tile.

The SRAM capacities per tile (L1) and per cluster (L2) are not revealed. If I had to guess – and I do – there is around 400 MB of SRAM cache spread across the compute tile at the center of the Clea chip package and another 200 MB embedded in the I/O chiplets to help cache network data as it enters and compute data as it exits the package.

There could be logic as well as SRAM embedded in the HBM controller dies, which are relatively large, as you can see. I am guessing that there is 200 MB of SRAM in the two I/O dies on the Clea package.

Across the Clea complex, I reckon that there is about 166.2 TB/sec of aggregate SRAM bandwidth, which counterbalances the 18 TB/sec of HBM memory bandwidth for the eight HBM4 stacks on the device. The Clea XPU has 288 GB of HBM 4, which is presumably from SK Hynix as was the case with the Braga XPU.

As for area and transistor count for the Clea package, you can make a rough estimate based on the fact that HBM memory sizes are known and we have images of the chip packages for all three Maia chips as well as their process nodes. I assume, by the way, that the HBM memory controller and I/O dies used in Clea are using 5 nanometer, not 2 nanometer, processes, which would make them perform better and also be more cheaply made. (Shrinking I/O circuits does not necessarily improve their performance, and it most definitely raises their costs and shrinks their yield.) It looks like the Clea package is about 1,980 mm 2 in area, which is 2.4X times as large as I think the Braga package was, at 810 mm 2 in area. Playing around with some numbers, I peg the transistor count at around 280 billion, give or take maybe 10 percent, not including the HBM4 memory.

Take a look for yourself and make your own guesses:

Here are the feeds and speeds for all three Maia XPUs, with estimates by me made in bright red bold italics as usual:

Microsoft has not said who its chip shepherd is for the Maia 300, but Global UniChip (GUC) of Taiwan, a close packaging partner of TSMC (which owns 35 percent of the company), was said to be the shepherd for Maia 100 a few years back. Everyone presumes that GUC is shepherding Maia 200 and Maia 300, although there were rumors two years ago that Marvell was trying to muscle in on the Maia line and, soon thereafter, there were rumors that Broadcom was trying to geta piece of the Microsoft custom silicon biz.

As was the case with the Braga XPU, the Clea XPU interlinks four accelerator motherboards together and puts them into a server form factor. With Braga, the CPU hosts were outside of XPU racks. But with the Clea XPUs, the host server – which we presume in both cases is a 132-core Cobalt 200 series Arm server CPU designed by Microsoft and shepherded in some fashion by Arm itself – is pulled inside of the CPU node. In either case, we assume the CPUs and XPUs are linked with PCI-Express switches, not Ethernet ports. But, maybe not.

Microsoft may pick another CPU chip shepherd now that Arm is selling its own AGI processor. Hence the rumors about Broadcom last year.

Here is what the Maia 300 server looks like:

If you squint, it looks very similar to the Maia 100 and Maia 200 servers, with the CPU pulled inside the chassis. But there are more differences than meet the eye. All three Maia generations are wired together differently. Here is how the Maia 100 RoCE Ethernet wired accelerators to each other within a node and then out to a two-level network to each other across a rack:

Nine of the twelve 400 Gb/sec links were used to link a quad of Maia 100s very tightly to each other, and three of the remaining links were used to hook into a three-plane Ethernet fabric that was the first tier of the network (which is T0 of course). This first tier could interlink 32 accelerators to each other, and a second tier of Ethernet switches were used to scale the system out to 576 nodes and 2,304 Athena XPUs in a single coherency domain.

With the Maia 200, the I/O portion of the chip implemented 28 Ethernet ports running at 400 Gb/sec for a total of 2.8 TB/sec of aggregate, bi-directional bandwidth. Here is how most of those ports were used:

There are four switch planes in this ATL 1.0 network, so that burns four ports per accelerator. Interestingly, Microsoft once again tightly coupled a quad of Maia 200s into a shared memory system with lots of bandwidth between the devices, with each Maia 200 connected to others with seven ports excepting one per chip that was used to link into the first plane (Switch Plane 0) in the diagram. That’s a total of 20 ports for linking the XPUs to each other and another four to link each XPU into each of the four planes for a total of 24 out of the 28 total ports. I have no idea where the other four ports are used. Perhaps they link the memory of the CPU host coherently with the accelerators using the ESUN or UALoE protocols?

What I can see is that a dozen trays of four Braga XPUs comprises a rack with 48 devices, and up to 128 racks can be interlinked into the coherency domain with 128 first tier (Tier 0) switches and 32 second tier (Tier 1) switches to span 6,144 XPUs in a single currency domain. These Ethernet switches have 51.2 Tb/sec ASICs and have 128 ports in total running at 400 Gb/sec.

Here is the important thing: the Braga device was set up to share all of its HBM memory across all of its compute tiles and the Braga system board tightly coupled four of these XPUs to also share their memory in a NUMA fashion.

With the Maia 300, a pair of compute tiles is tied to a pair of HBM4 memory banks in a NUMA-ish way. Meaning, memory is not shared across all tiles and all HBM4 stacks on the socket explicitly. This will make routines that fit into that memory bank run faster, which is important for GenAI inference. As you will see soon in my analysis of the OpenAI “Jalapeno” AI accelerator, which I am finishing up now, this is a tack that OpenAI and Broadcom did in the Jalapeno design, too. As I have been warned by some techies, I over-value coherence. Apparently Microsoft did, too.

So, with the Maia 300, only two accelerators are linked to each other, instead of four, as well as there being four distinct memory HBM4 regions within the Clea package. Here is what it all looks like, with the ATL 2.0 network lashing it all together:

Microsoft has a next generation of liquid cooling for the Maia 300 racks, and is moving from a 2U form factor to a 1U form factor, which allows it to double up the number of XPUs per rack to 96 by having two dozen servers instead of a dozen. Across 128 racks, that gives you 12,288 accelerators in a single system image. Like this:

That is the biggest coherency domain we have heard of yet across the big cloud builders, and a heck of a lot larger than the 72 or 144 GPU coherency domains that Nvidia and AMD are doing in a coherent fashion across their rackscale systems, or even the 576 or 1,152 multi-tiered NVSwitch coherent fabrics that Nvidia is promising for production environments in the future. Google’s “Sunfish” TPU 8t training chip (which is not yet shipping) tops out at 9,600 TPUs in a coherency domain, while the “Zebrafish” TPU 8i inference chip has a “boardfly” topology that peaks at 32 in a boardfly (a dragonfly topology of eight dragonfly nodes with four TPUs per node) and 1,152 in a group of 36 boardflies linked to each other over the “Apollo” optical circuit switch that is the backend for the Google network.

To save you from having to do the rack math, Microsoft did it for you here:

These are raw feeds and speeds, of course, and are not necessarily what happens when real applications run. What Microsoft’s top techie brass – Rani Borkar , president of Azure Hardware Systems and Infrastructure, and Saurabh Dighe , corporate vice president of Systems Planning and Architecture – said in their deep dive is that Maia 300 with 96 XPUs in a rack delivers up to 7X the “token throughput” performance of a rack of Maia 200s with 48 XPUs in a rack. You get 36 percent more flops moving from Maia 200 to Maia 300, and then another 100 percent from the XPU count doubling in the rack.

The real difference here has to be architecture, by coupling the XPUs and nodes in the system differently, having more HBM and SRAM memory and a lot more bandwidth at all stages of the calculations. And the dataflow that moves information around the system so it can be processed and created is no doubt a big, big part of the improvement. We look forward to the paper that will come out a year from now telling us how Microsoft did it.

Here is the metric that Microsoft is likely most proud of: You get that 7X performance improvement with a 2.5X improvement in performance per watt. It is easy – well, relatively easy – to get more performance by throwing more power at things. It is another thing to do it while increasing the power efficiency.

item.title: Upscale AI Partners With Nvidia While Competing With It
item.description:
Every CPU maker always had its own and very proprietary way to link multiple CPUs into shared memory clusters and for the most part, this remains true despite the efforts of the CCIX consortium and even the CXL consortium to create a kind of universal glue to make many CPUs look like one much bigger CPU.

Attempts to create CPU SMP and NUMA standards largely failed because as much as customers would have liked to have a standard way to link CPUs together, the odds that they had a workload that would mix and match CPUs of different architectures from different vendors together seemed small. Moreover, each vendor could innovate on their SMP and NUMA chipsets, which were eventually embedded in the CPUs themselves, at a pace that was distinct from advances in their core designs, memory subsystems, and I/O. And most importantly, they were not dependent on some standards body to approve features they needed and they could differentiate as they saw fit.

So why do we think there will be a standard version of what amounts to a NUMA interconnect – what is commonly called scale up networking these days – for GPUs and XPUs? Because hope springs eternal, and because markets love competition because it drives down costs. (Substitution is a law of economics, not just a good idea. . . .)

What is clear is that Nvidia can – and does – charge a hefty premium for its NVSwitch and NVLink ports, which offer unparalleled bandwidth and decent latency to glue as many as 72 GPUs to each other as a shared memory system that the company calls the NVL72 rackscale machine. With its NVLink Fusion effort , Nvidia is allowing those making custom CPUs to add NVLink ports to their devices so they can hook into the same memory space as Nvidia GPUs, and is similarly allowing XPU accelerators made by hyperscalers, cloud builders, and AI model builders to have NVLink ports so they can be put inside Nvidia’s rackscale architecture. Thus far, as far as we know, Nvidia is not allowing customers to add NVLink ports to both their own CPUs and their own XPUs and just buy NVSwitches and a license to the NVLink protocol from Nvidia to make shared memory systems.

That day might come, though, as I talked about in August in In The Long Run, Nvidia NVSwitch Is The InfiniBand Of Scale Up AI Networks . And in the longest of runs, should the right technology come to the market, Nvidia could adopt an industry standard scale up network with its own protocol overlays – particularly when it comes to AI inference. (There is no reason for Nvidia to yield such ground for AI training, where it has the vast majority of the market locked up.)

This is why Upscale AI, which I talked to back in January as it was raising $200 million in Series A funding , is so interesting. (I am not going to go over the history of the company here, and the serious players involved, so read that story if you want the background.) Upscale AI has raised $500 million in total so far, and its valuation has doubled to $2 billion and its employee count has also more than doubled to over 300 people since that January announcement. This week, the top brass at Upscale AI raised the curtain a little bit more on its plans for scale up and scale out networking aimed specifically at AI clusters.

Before you get too excited, we did not get much in the way of speeds and feeds for the “SkyHammer” scale up switch ASIC that has been in development for several years. Rajiv Khemani , co-founder and executive chairman at Upscale AI, and Barun Kar , its chief executive officer, have long and deep experience in high performance systems and networking, so we expect some interesting twists.

UPSCALE AI SKYHAMMER SKYFABRIX

What we do know from reading that slide from a webinar – that’s Arvind Srikumar , senior vice president of product and marketing at the company, giving that part of the presentation – is that SkyHammer will have an aggregate bandwidth of 115.2 Tb/sec, which is state of the art and stands toe to toe with the best from Cisco Systems, Broadcom, and Nvidia for their scale out network ASICs. The chart also says that the SkyHammer chips and the SkyFabriX architecture it supports will eventually have switch gear that spans multiple petabits per second of aggregate bandwidth.

This will very likely be accomplished by ganging up multiple SkyHammer ASICs inside of a switch, much as Broadcom and Cisco often do for both fixed port and modular switches. As you know from watching the Broadcom and Meta Platforms presentations over the past decade in The Next Platform , you can double the bandwidth of ports with any given switch ASIC architecture by creating a baby two-tier network from six independent ASICs. Half the bandwidth of four of the ASICs are used to create downlinks, and the other half are used to cross-couple the four ASICs together using a pair of the same chips. This obviously doubles the latency for many of the port hops through the switch, but not for all of them. You can also use specialized fabric connectors (like the “Ramon” devices that are paired with Broadcom’s “Jericho” deep buffer ASICs) to create even larger modular switches.

Upscale AI will no doubt also create devices with higher aggregate bandwidth, and that is because the economics works out. You can build a switch with 2X the native bandwidth per port out of six switch ASICs, but it costs around 1.5X per port to do it compared to making a single device with 2X the bandwidth. (That is street pricing, not the cost of making the ASICs.) The company did not provide a roadmap for future SkyHammer ASICs.

As far as memory domain scalability goes, the SkyHammer chip’s architecture can support up to 576 accelerators in a single networking tier, and just like NVSwitch, using multiple network tiers it can scale further – in this case, to “thousands of accelerators.” How many thousands remains to be seen, but 1,024 or 1,156 seem to be the two numbers to aim for. The UALink consortium is promising 1,024 XPUs in a single tier , and Nvidia is going to try to scale NVSwitch beyond its current 576 GPU limit to 1,152 GPUs in the “Rubin Ultra” GPU generation. (This is with a multi-tier network, not a single tier.) Nvidia supports 72 GPUs in a single domain now, with 576 GPUs being possible with multiple tiers but not intended for production workloads.

If you do the math on that 576 devices number for SkyHammer, each device is getting 200 Gb/sec of bandwidth. This is obviously a lot less than the 1.8 TB/sec that an NVSwitch 5/NVLink 5 generation offers on the “Grace-Blackwell” NVL72 systems. The “Vera-Rubin” NVL72 systems will have NVSwitch 6/NVLink 6 with 3.6 TB/sec. With 72 XPUs, SkyHammer is delivering 1.6 Tb/sec per port, which is still only 200 GB/sec of memory bandwidth over the scale up network. That is one-sixth that of the NVSwitch 5 stack. (I have normalized the NVSwitch names

It is not at all clear that bandwidth matters more than latency, particularly for AI inference workloads. And predictable latency is always more important than low latency, as Google has taught us.

“One of the most important metrics when it comes to tokens is latency,” Srikumar tells The Next Platform . “We have to produce, but this is where it's a little bit different from what Rajiv and Barun has done in the past. With AI, the latency has to be super predictable, and we have built into the ASIC predictable jitter. And at the same time, transmission reliability within the domain is also important. We have some protocols which are standards-based that provide link level reliability, but within the fabric we have a mechanism to ensure the fabric is 100 percent lossless. This is why we call it reliable and predictable latency, where we are minimizing the latency. And you might be surprised with the numbers once we announce the specifics, If you look at a lot of Ethernet fabrics, there are pretty much a fixed pipeline arrangement, and it's a pipeline arrangement with less parallelism. Here we are doing a lot of things that are pushing the envelope on what has been done in the Ethernet fabrics to date. We believe SkyFabriX is going to be uniquely positioned in the market because we started with a clean sheet of paper rather than taking an Ethernet fabric and retrofitting the protocols that are needed for scale up.”

No matter what anyone believes, we are about to find out what works and what does not as people begin putting the UALink over Ethernet (UALoE in the common parlance today) and the ESUN memory protocols on top of fast Ethernet switches that have been tweaked to do scale up.

It is interesting to note that SkyHammer is running UALoE, not UALink proper, and the fact that it is running ESUN shows you that under the covers SkyHammer is an Ethernet switch ASIC. I was hoping that it was going to be a faster switch ASIC with more radix that could run UALink native and run an emulated version of ESUN when necessary. But, so it goes.

Here is the neat bit. Upscale AI has partnered with Nvidia to be its supplier of choice for scale out fabrics, and is choosing the Spectrum-X Ethernet switches in particular. Obviously not the Quantum-X InfiniBand switches, since the company’s founders are big believers in Ethernet eventually conquering InfiniBand. Some would say with the first generation of Ethernet switches that are compatible with the Ultra Ethernet Consortium’s specifications, this goal will be accomplished after nearly three decades of InfiniBand setting the high performance standard. InfiniBand will still beat the crap out of Ethernet when it comes to port-to-port hop latency. But Ethernet can get closer, and can scale out a lot further than InfiniBand for a given network topology. And Nvidia will be selling InfiniBand like crazy for those who need the lowest latency for their HPC and AI workloads. Fear not.

To be specific, Upscale AI will be acquiring Nvidia’s Spectrum-X ASICs and building its own scale-out switches from them as well as porting its SkyOS network operating system that runs on the scale up SkyFabriX switches so it also runs on the Spectrum-X ASICs. The reason this is possible is that SkyOS is an AI-optimized version of the SONiC network operating system and its related Switch Abstraction Interface (SAI) created by Microsoft way back in 2016 and which has become a de facto standard in many hyperscaler and cloud builder datacenters . The Upscale AI versions of Spectrum-X will support 400 Gb/sec, 800 Gb/sec, and 1.6 Tb/sec ports.

The important thing, according to Upscale AI, is that SkyOS will span both scale up and scale out networks, and its SkyCMD telemetry and orchestration tool will see both networks as a whole. The other important thing is that customers will be able to use any CPU or any GPU or any XPU front-ended by a DPU or NIC and will be able to mix and match these devices to create AI clusters. That is all well and good except that Nvidia is not supporting SkyHammer and its SkyOS as an alternative to NVSwitch for scale up. There is no way – as yet – to do scale up with Nvidia GPUs. AMD is actually counting on companies like Upscale AI to provide scale up networking options supporting UALink, UALoE, or ESUN, and it may lose patience and just acquire Upscale AI to own one of the options and make money from it. ( Why not? AMD is rich in stock funny money, and it may as well spend some of it.)

One last thing: Nvidia can always cut back on the bandwidth per port in an NVSwitch ASIC and increase the radix of the switch so it can flatten its NVSwitch network. But it will have to sacrifice bandwidth to do that. It might be faster to port the NVLink protocol to SkyHammer. . . . and have Nvidia become the dominant supplier of UALoE or ESUN switchery. We shall see.

item.title: SPONSORED: Growing pains: how distributed AI training changes the network between datacenters
item.description:
Large-scale AI training has already escaped the confines of a single datacenter. Google said Gemini was trained synchronously across clusters in multiple locations; Microsoft has connected AI data centres in Wisconsin and Georgia into what it describes as one distributed AI supercomputer; AWS has connected AI compute clusters across wide areas to allow Anthropic to build Claude models; Meta has built high-capacity datacenter interconnects to support model training ; and CoreWeave and Google Cloud recently announced cross-cloud training with a private interconnect, with Azure likely to follow later in the year.

This growing geographic spread of model training is partly due to the limits of single datacenters or campus clusters, which can be strained as they try to meet the compute and power demands of new models. Cisco estimates that training models today can require clusters with tens of thousands of GPUs. By 2030, the largest individual frontier training runs could draw 4-16GW of power , according to researchers at Epoch AI. Distributing compute allows hyperscalers and datacenter operators to build in locations with more available power or space and fewer planning constraints.

How To Train An LLM

At the core of an LLM is a neural network with billions of numerical parameters, or weights, that are adjusted during training. A batch of training data passes through the model, which makes a prediction. The system measures the error and calculates how the weights should change. The weights are updated and the process starts again. At the scale of modern models, this work is distributed across thousands of GPUs and other accelerators, such as AWS Trainium and Google TPUs.

Different GPUs can process separate batches of data or different parts of the model. But they cannot work entirely independently: at various points they must exchange results and synchronize before the next stage of training can begin.

What networks carry between the accelerators is generally not the text or images used to train the model, but large arrays of numerical data such as gradients and intermediate results. Thousands of accelerators may need to exchange and combine that data at roughly the same time.

"If you look at any training job, it is basically a repetition of compute and synchronization," explains Ramesh Sivakolundu of Cisco's Silicon One architecture team. "You compute the weights, communicate those weights to synchronize every GPU in the cluster, and then restart the computation. That means bursty traffic happens periodically throughout the training process."

Thousands of accelerators can finish a computation phase and start communicating at the same time. This can lead to "incast" problems where many senders converge on the same destination and traffic arrives faster than the next link can handle.

The fundamental issue lies with synchronization. In a synchronous training job, one group of GPUs cannot simply ignore a slower group and continue independently. The network-wide exchange must complete before the participating GPUs can move on to the next stage. A network delay therefore becomes compute delay.

"You don't want the network to be the bottleneck in the training process," says Sivakolundu. "The idea is to keep the GPUs fully occupied and not have the network introduce additional latency into the overall training program."

That does not mean that every instance of network congestion or packet loss brings the entire model training to a complete halt. However, a delayed or dropped flow may require retransmission, prolong a collective communication operation, and leave other accelerators waiting. More serious failures can require training to return to a saved checkpoint.

Different Kind Of Interconnect

"Inside a single datacenter, you can assume you have built a full network connecting the GPU racks with the bandwidth you planned for," says Itamar Gold, director of product management at Cisco. Gold’s point is that with scale-across, coordinated AI workloads may have to traverse a more constrained inter-site fabric than the network within each facility. Instead, he says, traffic destined for the other facility may be funneled through what is effectively a narrower pipe. A synchronized burst can turn that pipe into a temporary choke point.

Traditional DCI connects otherwise independent datacenter environments, and is typically built for redundancy, reach and workload distribution. The traffic that runs over them is often replication traffic or application data, and the flows are asynchronous, meaning one flow does not have to finish in lockstep with the others.

In scale-across AI training, the inter-site network becomes part of a coordinated distributed computation rather than simply moving data between otherwise independent systems. It is therefore essential to have sufficient bandwidth and predictable delivery.

From Rack To Region

Within a rack, bandwidth requirements can be enormous – up to 800 Gb/sec and 1.6 Tb/sec – but the distances are short. High-speed serial lanes combine to make a GPU cluster appear as a single compute unit. When the AI fabric is extended across an entire facility, “scale out” racks will still require connections up to 1.6 Tb/sec. At these data rates, copper is generally confined to short reaches. Connections across rack rows and datacenter floors instead use pluggable optics, with scale-out links extending from hundreds of meters to around 2km.

“Scale-across” extends a coordinated AI fabric across multiple facilities, making inter-site network behavior part of workload performance. Depending on the architecture, those links may span metro or regional distances, and potentially farther depending on the architecture. According to Cisco modelling of large distributed AI deployments, aggregate bandwidth requirements can reach roughly 14x a conventional DCI baseline.

For starters, short-range datacenter optics are not designed to carry 400-800 Gbps signals over hundreds of kilometers. For these distances, operators need coherent optics that use sophisticated modulation and high-performance digital signal processing to keep high-rate optical signals usable over metro and regional fiber spans, compensating for physical impairments that become more pronounced with distance. The number of ports matters too. Cisco estimates that connecting two 100 megawatt AI sites could require 12,000 to 32,000 coherent optical ports at the scale-across layer, compared with roughly 1,000 to 2,000 for conventional DCI between comparable facilities. At 400 Gb/sec or 800 Gb/sec per port, that adds up to multi-petabit aggregate capacity.

Moving that much data is also a power and space problem. Coherent pluggables put the coherent transponder function directly into router or switch ports, avoiding a separate bank of standalone DWDM transponders. Cisco says this reduces the additional rack space, power and cooling needed for the inter-site optical layer which is an important consideration when the AI factories themselves are already power-constrained.

The Latency Problem

Even with sufficient bandwidth and suitable optics, distance adds latency. If congestion develops, the network needs time to signal the sender to slow down. Over a local AI fabric, feedback can arrive quickly. However, if the connection is stretched across 100 kilometers of fiber, considerably more data can be transmitted before the sender even learns that there is a problem.

Cisco calculates that on an 800 Gb/sec connection spanning 100 kilometers, around 100 MB of data can already be in transit during that feedback interval. Cisco argues that these longer feedback loops increase the value of networking silicon designed with substantially deeper buffering. The shallow-buffer switching architectures designed for very low latency inside a datacenter have less capacity to absorb traffic while congestion feedback crosses a long-distance link.

"The reason you need deeper buffers as the distances get longer is that you don't get feedback about the transfer of packets for a longer period of time," says Sivakolundu. "If you don't buffer deeply enough, you can end up dropping and retransmitting packets, increasing latency."

Deep buffering absorbs a temporary burst or disruption while traffic management and congestion signaling address the underlying problem. Sustained congestion still needs more capacity or a change in how traffic is distributed.

The same buffer also helps with oversubscription. If the combined capacity feeding into an inter-site connection is greater than the capacity of the link itself, a synchronized burst can arrive faster than the link can drain it. Buffering gives that excess traffic somewhere to wait without getting dropped while congestion controls respond.

Rather than dividing the available buffer into fixed amounts for each port, a shared buffer is a common pool of packet memory that can be allocated wherever congestion appears. That lets a busy link absorb a larger burst without dropping packets.

"The longer you're reaching out, the more you may need to buffer," says Gold. "You also need the flexibility to put as much buffer as possible where it is needed, perhaps on one port or a few ports where you've identified a problematic flow. Our approach is a single, fully shared buffer."

AI training does offer one useful characteristic: much of its collective communication is repetitive and therefore more predictable than DCI traffic. Cisco's approach is to use proactive congestion management to steer or schedule traffic before a predictable burst creates a problem, while retaining deep buffering as a safety net for transient congestion and unpredictable events such as a link failure. The two approaches are complementary: one tries to avoid the queue while the other gives the network somewhere to put the traffic when a queue forms.

Cisco’s Bet On Co-Design

Cisco’s scale-across architecture uses the Silicon One P200, a 51.2 Tb/sec programmable, deep-buffer routing processor included in the Cisco 8223 and Cisco N9000 platforms. Those systems can be paired with Cisco's 400G and 800G coherent pluggable optics for the long-distance links, while open line systems such as Cisco Open Transport 3000 and Cisco NCS 1014 handle the optical transport layer where required.

Coherent pluggables generate the DWDM wavelengths directly from the routing system, while the line system amplifies and carries those wavelengths across the fiber plant. For links requiring multiple parallel fiber pairs, Cisco's Open Transport 3000 uses a multi-rail design that combines the optical components for multiple rails onto one line card. Cisco claims this reduces power per rail by 75 percent and rack space by 80 percent. Where a separate transport system is required, the NCS 1014 can provide 12.8 Tb/sec of capacity from a 1RU line card.

The P200 has a programmable run-to-completion network processor and P4 tooling, which Cisco says allows protocol support, telemetry and other packet-processing features to be developed in software rather than making every change dependent on a new silicon generation.

For scale-across, where operators are still testing different topologies and traffic-management methods, "the same programmable flexibility can let network functions evolve without every new requirement forcing a chip replacement,” says Sivakolundu.

Cisco also includes hardware-based protection for inter-site traffic in that design, its argument being that encryption should not create another processing bottleneck for the training fabric.

A key part of Cisco's pitch is the co-design. A networking ASIC is defined years before the finished router reaches a datacenter. Cisco argues that because its silicon, system and optics teams sit within the same company, requirements for port density, buffering, power, telemetry and the optical interfaces can feed back into the chip design rather than the system team receiving a commercial ASIC and working out what it can build around it.

That does not mean scale-across has settled on a single approved architecture. Cisco itself divides the problem into campus, metro, and regional deployments, and different operators are experimenting with various combinations of networking and training techniques.

Implementations vary significantly by operator, including distance, topology and workload design, while the common problem is maintaining coordinated AI performance across sites. The technology is still at an early stage, however. "We are seeing early deployments now, but it is a process and I think it will take a few years," says Gold.

Designing a network for distributed training will not eliminate the latency of distance, but it can keep that interconnect from becoming the bottleneck. That gives hyperscalers and datacenter operators the flexibility to add compute where power and space are available, while still treating multiple sites as part of the same training infrastructure.

item.title: Memory Is The Lynchpin Of The IT Industry, And Doubly So For AI
item.description:
For as long as most of us have been watching high-end commercial and technical computing, the compute part of the system – the CPU for five decades then also GPUs for the past decade and a half – has been, without a doubt, the focal point of the system. Memory, storage, and I/O were always important, but they were secondary.

Budgets for systems and clusters were focused on maximizing compute, and these other factors were often secondary. And to be honest, organizations sometimes skimped on memory and I/O to the detriment of driving CPU or GPU utilization.

With the advent of machine learning and its evolution into generative AI and then agentic AI, memory has come front and center and has eclipsed compute as the control point in most of the IT sector. This is a bit disorienting for many of us, not so much in the concept of the change but in the rapidity of the magnitude of the change.

Here is the latest chip revenue breakdown from Gartner that shows memory versus non-memory sales, and flash is considered memory as far as the market researcher is concerned:

As you can see, the semiconductor market overall is on a Moore’s Law curve of sorts, doubling revenues every year. Call it More’s Law, if you will. The nearly doubling happened between 2025 and 2026, but as you can see, the forecasts show the growth rate decelerating between 2026 and 2027 – something we have been saying was inevitable since the GenAI boom. At some point, competition kicks in, and at another point, people have enough capacity to do what they need to do.

I estimated the breakdown between DRAM and NAND flash, which you can solve given the growth rates that Gartner gave in its statement for 2026 for these two categories. I assume the other types of memory are worth about $4 billion or so a year and are growing at 2X global gross domestic product, which legacy components and platforms tend to do.

I also added in Micron’s latest total addressable market forecast for HBM memory so we can back out other kinds of DRAM – DDR4 and DDR5, LPDDR4 and LPDDR5, and so on – from the mix. As you can see, the implied other DRAM revenues will dwarf the sales of HBM, probably for the foreseeable future.

The demand for DRAM main memory, HBM stacked memory, and flash storage – which commercial companies have adopted instead of disk drives as they try to “scale in” the performance of their workloads – is off the charts, and not just because GenAI is a memory and flash hog.
