We are in a massive upgrade cycle for systems, which need to be upgraded because machines that are five, six, or seven years old sitting out there in the server fleets of the world need to be upgraded. And to save space and power for AI systems, companies are going for near-maximum density of cores, and that is in turn driving demand for high capacity DRAM and flash. The traditional IT sector – transaction processing, data warehousing, data analytics, and web infrastructure – finds itself competing against the tech titans and their humungous GenAI aspirations for flash and DRAM memory. And DRAM supplies are tightening as memory makers shift their DRAM chip capacity to making HBM stacked memory for AI accelerators to chase higher revenues (but not necessarily higher profits).

This has made DRAM prices go bonkers. Back in November 2022, when OpenAI’s ChatGPT started the GenAI boom, DDR4 memory cost around $3 per GB for servers and DDR5 memory cost around $4 per GB. (These prices are averages across midrange capacities. Denser memory costs a hell of a lot more per GB, and skinnier memory costs considerably less.) A 30 TB TLC enterprise SSD cost somewhere around 10 cents to 13 cents per GB. Four years later, the street price of DDR4 server memory is from 2X to 3X more expensive at the street price, DDR5 server memory is anywhere from 9X to 13X higher, and that 30 TB TLC SSD will run you 6X to 7X more. Some of that change, by the way, was due to a memory and flash price crash that hit in late 2021, due to the oversupply issues that have plagued the memory and flash businesses for many decades.

And by the way, disk drive prices have skyrocketed, too. A 30 TB nearline disk drive costs about 2.5X over the same span, and if you think you can buy cheap disk, forget about it because the hyperscalers and cloud builders have contracted the vast majority of disk drive supplies from Seagate, Western Digital, and Toshiba, the three remaining disk drive makers.

HBM is a little different. First of all, there are three makers of HBM stacked DRAM memory – Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology – and there are no spot prices because the market is not open but dedicated to two GPU makers (Nvidia and AMD) and XPU makers and/or their chip shepherds. So pricing information is a little sketchy.

Back when HBM2 debuted in 2017, the rumor was that it cost around $20 per GB, but this settled down to around $8 per GB two years later. With HBM2E, which provided a bandwidth bump, it was around $10 per GB, rising to around $12 per GB for HBM3, which had more capacity per stack and more bandwidth, and the HBM3E with a bandwidth boost cost around $13.50 per GB. The HBM4 that will start shipping in the next generation of GPUs and XPUs, it is rumored to cost around $16 per GB – the rumor is actually that Nvidia’s contract price is $560 to $600 per 36 GB stack. For some reason, some people are expecting for HBM4E, which has a substantial bandwidth bump, to cost twice as much per GB as HBM4. I am not sure I believe that, given the trend data above for HBM2 through HBM4 memory. I can see $20 per GB, but $36 per GB is tough to fathom, even with the benefits.

Here is the thing to remember: The cost per GB of finished HBM parts is only up 1.6X since the GenAI boom started, while the number of DRAM chips that get tossed into the garbage because of perfectly normal but below 100 percent yields happen in manufacturing is increasing with each passing generation. The idea out there is that HBM makers will raise the price on HBM4E in 2027 to get the profitability of HBM more in line with standard DRAM.

By the way, these HBM costs above are not what end users pay to get the HBM memory on their devices, unlike the DRAM and flash prices above. The cost of the HBM to users as they buy GPUs and XPUs is much higher than the price that the vendors pay to get, as I explained in He Who Can Pay Top Dollar For HBM Memory Controls AI Training back in February 2024. The HBM memory probably represents half the cost to under users of a GPU from Nvidia and AMD, and is probably closer to 65 percent of the cost of an XPU accelerator made by the hyperscalers, cloud builders, or AI model builders now that OpenAI has entered the fray with its “Jalapeno” AI accelerator.

Here’s the thing. I have heard all the rumors about how GPU and XPU makers (and designers) are trying to do more with the HBM they can get allocated. Some are sticking with more stacks of HBM3E instead of moving to HBM4, maintaining most of the memory bandwidth – important for the decode part of inference – even as they sacrifice some of the memory capacity.

Nvidia is rumored to be backing away from its initial plans for the “Rubin Ultra” GPU coming in 2027, which was supposed to have four reticle-limited GPU chiplets and up to 1 TB of HBM4E memory. AMD is holding at 488 GB for its “Altair” MI455X GPU accelerator, while Nvidia is said to be considering going as low as 192 GB on some future Rubin and Rubin Ultra designs.

What seems more likely is that Nvidia will move the HBM controller off the GPU chiplet and onto the customizable base die that is possible with HBM4 and HBM4E designs – what Nvidia calls NVHBM but which is in no way unique to Nvidia. Others will have custom base dies for their HBM stacks, and more than a few will embed certain mathematical functions in there like processor in memory or PIM has been doing for a decade (without any market traction) to make some of the stuff happen in memory instead of being dragged across the memory channel into the GPU or XPU.

Here is why these custom base dies in the HBM stack matter, as Nvidia explains: “By integrating the memory controller into the 3D HBM stack instead of the XPU, NVHBM delivers up to 30 percent greater memory bandwidth and 15 percent lower HBM power consumption, and frees up to 25 percent more area on XPU compute die compared with standard HBM4E.”

If I was a betting man, I would put my chips on the idea that Rubin Ultra will make use of that extra 25 percent of freed-up chip area per chiplet to add more performance across two chiplets and maybe deliver 512 GB of HBM4E memory, maybe 384 GB with the same bandwidth. The original Rubin Ultra had four stacks per GPU chiplet, which were sixteen chips high at 4 GB a pop to reach that 1,024 GB capacity and, given the specs on the Samsung stacks, a whopping 58 TB/sec of aggregate memory bandwidth. By cutting down the stack heights and slicing the chiplet count in two, you can maintain 28 TB/sec of bandwidth and have 256 GB (eight high), 384 GB (twelve high), or 512 GB (sixteen high) of capacity.

All GPU and XPU makers are looking at similar choices when what they really want is the maximum HBM capacity and bandwidth for their devices on the leading edge technology at a much lower price per GB.

item.title: HPE Unveils The First Of The Next Generation of ProLiants for the AI Era
item.description:
It is impossible to miss the impact that the rapid adoption of AI continues to have on the datacenter infrastructure space and everything that goes with it – power consumption and costs, for example – both over the past few years and in projections into the next decade.

In a report released late last month , Bain & Co analysts predict that by 2031, annual spending on AI infrastructure could hit $1.5 trillion, which includes everything from new datacenter infrastructure and compute capacity to GPU upgrades, memory, and networking hardware. Power capacity, which in the most advanced AI datacenters is nearing 1 gigawatt, could double by next year and power past 9 GW by the end of the decade.

The ravenous appetite among hyperscalers for infrastructure continues to grow, with capital spending from the likes of Microsoft , Amazon , Google , Oracle , and Meta expected to hit $780 billion this year, or about five times the amount from just three years ago, they wrote.

OEMs understand this and are rolling out datacenter systems aimed at feeding the AI beast. The latest example comes this week, with Hewlett Packard Enterprise unveiling the first of its ProLiant Gen 13 systems with greater compute, memory, and networking capabilities for enterprise AI inferencing and agentic workloads and a focus on such areas as security, performance, and reliability, which always have been important in datacenter systems but can take on greater roles with AI workloads.

The first four 13 th generation ProLiants are aimed at the highest performing dense computing and GPU workloads, John Carter, vice president of product management for HPE Compute, tells The Next Platform . Those include traditional enterprises trying to get the most performance out of their infrastructure or companies that are pushing what can be done with agentic AI and big model simulation.

“That kind of scale and performance brings new security risks,” Carter says. “It brings new complexity in terms of managing many, many systems. We're talking about companies taking their most core critical IP and data and now putting it into these kinds of LLMs [large language models] and simulations and this kind of stuff. That's critical to be secure. The management and security that we've continued to bring from multiple generations here becomes even more important because it really lays that foundational silicon level root-of-trust to allow a build into the other levels of the infrastructure.”

Given that, what HPE is doing this week is both unveiling the latest generation of ProLiant systems as well as improvements in the software that manages and protects them. Common to all of the new systems is the use of AMD’s 6 th Gen Epyc 9006 SP7 “Venice” CPUs, which the chipmaker released in July.

Anchoring the new systems is the ProLiant DL585a, a 10U server that can hold up to eight double-wide GPUs from Nvidia, AMD, or Intel and two of the latest AMD Epyc CPUs, which offer up to 256 cores each. The system also includes sixth-generation PCI connectivity. The server, which will be available in March 2027, is built to accommodate current and future power and thermal demands and address the growing token throughput and PCIe needs of such AI workloads as inferencing, retrieval augmented generation (RAG), and agentic AI, according to Carter.

“Most of our customers who are using a PCIe-type GPU, what they're really telling us is, ‘We’re running out of power long before we run out of space, so make it bigger,’” he says. “We want to keep air cooling, so that's really where this is positioned. This is more for the enterprise, for the mid-tier service providers, those kinds of folks.”

The ProLiant DL525, which becomes available next month, is single-socket and air-cooled 1U system with a single 256-core AMD chip with high-bandwidth, 16-chnanel memory, and support for both DDR5 and MRDIMM memory. The system is designed for high data-throughput workloads like AI inference, EDA, and fraud detection. It fits into standard 19-inch rack.

“Now we're shifting from GPU-focus to CPU-focus,” Carter says. “This is where we're going to talk more about the agentic side of the story, where we're expecting the ratio to shift from two to eight CPUs to GPUs, now more like one to one. The expectation here is as agentic gets bigger, our customers are going to need these kinds of dense CPU platforms as part of that workflow to offload many of the actions that just perform with their own CPU.”

The two new XD systems, both set for release next year, are follow-ons to what HPE in the past has referred to its Apollo 2000 or XD 2000 series, according to Carter.

“These new XD servers are now put into an open 21-inch ORV3 rack infrastructure part,” he says. “They sit in a wider and specialized rack. There are shared power and shared cooling capabilities between those systems to bring more efficiency. What you really get here is the ultimate density in compute. I can drive many, many, many cores in the same data space. It's really specialized for customers who have built modernized datacenters. . . so high density power to the rack, liquid cooling available or high-efficiency air cooling.”

Both the XD245 (below) and the XD285 are housed in a 2OU chassis, with the XD245 including four half-width dual-socket nodes compared with the XD285 having two such nodes. Each can run up to 256-core AMD CPUs, 16 memory channels per CPU, and MRDIMM support. The XD245 is liquid-cooled; the XD285 is cooled with air.

Weaved throughout these systems is enhanced management and security software, including in iLO 8. The improvements put a particular focus on security, a top-of-mind issue for organizations when it come to AI, and agentic AI in particular. iLO 8 offers HDD or SSD storage drives that automatically encrypt and decrypt the data that’s on the hardware from the moment the system boots. There also is multi-party authorization, which ensures high-impact actions by AI or agents, such as key provisioning and secure erase, have two authorized human n approvers, with Chris Bradley, director of mainstream computer customer advocacy and technical enablement at HPE, adding that they embedded it into individual nodes to work as rules within iLO.

HPE also expanded post-quantum cryptography (PQC), a security capability aimed at protecting data in the upcoming quantum computing era. Current encryption methods like AES-256 work well now, data protected by the technology will become more vulnerable when cybercriminals are able to use quantum computing’s much more powerful capabilities. A key worry now is what’s called “harvest now, decrypt later,” where threat actors are holding stolen data with plans to decrypt it when quantum computing becomes available to them.

HPE is “ensuring that we've got the both quantum cryptography algorithms and capabilities already in the management construct,” Bradley tells The Next Platform .

HPE’s newest ProLiant systems add to the rapidly growing infrastructure choices enterprises and HPC organizations have for their AI datacenters that the Bain analysts wrote about in September. But as they noted, there are cautions that need to be heeded in the rush.

“The unprecedented speed and scale of the AI buildout, with billions flowing into chips, data centers, networks, and power systems, have focused attention on the challenge of building capacity,” they wrote. “But the more important question may be whether enough economic value can be created to justify it.”

item.title: SPONSORED: When one datacenter is no longer enough
item.description:
Training the largest AI models is no longer simply a question of adding more GPUs. As clusters grow, power availability is becoming a hard physical constraint, forcing infrastructure teams to consider how a single training workload can operate across multiple data centres.

That creates a very different networking problem. Traditional datacenter interconnect was designed to move traffic between sites. AI training demands something more exacting: huge, synchronous flows, minimal packet loss and tightly coordinated communication between GPUs. If one part of the cluster stalls, the impact can ripple across the entire job.

In this interview, The Register’s Tim Phillips speaks with Rakesh Chopra, SVP, Silicon and Systems Architecture, Cisco Fellow , about what Cisco calls the “Scale-Across” imperative and why it believes distributed AI infrastructure requires a new approach to routing.

Rakesh explains how the demands of AI are changing the role of the network, from simple transport to an integral part of the compute system. He discusses the challenge of making geographically separate facilities behave more like a single deterministic machine, and why buffering, high-speed coherent optics and tightly integrated silicon matter when workloads span long-distance fiber links.

The conversation also looks inside the cluster itself. Rakesh outlines how Cisco’s Silicon One architecture and Intelligent Collective Networking are designed to manage synchronized bursts of GPU traffic, reduce bottlenecks and improve job completion time. Power efficiency is another central theme, including the trade-off between network consumption and the energy available to GPUs.

Security and longevity also come into focus. The interview covers hardware-accelerated MACsec and IPsec, as well as the role of programmability in helping infrastructure adapt as AI workloads continue to evolve.

For infrastructure and datacenter leaders planning for larger, more distributed AI environments, the discussion offers a practical view of the networking challenges that emerge once one site is no longer enough.

item.title: Dell Adds Data Context, Prep, And Storage Features To Its AI Data Platform
item.description:
Earlier this year, Dell published the results from a survey of 3,800 enterprise IT decision-makers and AI experts from around the world talking about their experiences in adopting and scaling the technology, how they use it and the accelerates they put in place. What the vendor was told was that data – including its quality, availability, management, and security – is the top challenge .

That didn’t surprise Dell executives, who since launching its AI Data Platform two years ago have been sounding that message that what’s tripping up organizations bringing AI into their operations is not so much GPUs or similar hardware situations but the data.

“This is the gap that we hear from customers every day,” Varun Chhabra , senior vice president of Dell’s Infrastructure Solutions Group, told journalists at a recent media briefing. “The infrastructure is ready, but the data isn't, and without data that's ready for AI, investments turn from isolated pilots and turn into isolated pilots that never really reach the full potential through scale to the rest of the organization. The real bottleneck is not access to compute, it's not often access to models. It's actually access to data. Enterprise data is just not in a place where it's ready to support scaling of AI workloads.”

AI needs a lot of data to scale, but much of that data is housed in different locations, from the cloud and datacenters to file systems, databases, applications, and edge locations, Chhabra said, adding that “much of it is trapped in silos, silos based on workloads, and there is often not a unified way to reach it. Much of is unstructured. It's often dark, which means it's effectively invisible to AI. It is often ungoverned, so the teams are stuck between AI that needs access and policies that require control.”

Through the AI Data Platform – a foundational element of the Dell’s AI Factory – the company is working to put the tools and capabilities in place to address the myriad data challenges. As seen below, the platform is essentially three layers, starting with the Data Orchestration Engine for taking in, preparing, labeling, and enriching data, complete with unified data pipelines, distributed control that decouples compute from storage, and native access to Nvidia NIM microservices , AI Blueprints , and templates.

The Data Engines for analytics, processing, and search helps organizations find the use the right data they need in hours instead of weeks, Chhabra said. Then come the Storage Engines that include PowerScale for network attached storage (NAS) for unstructured data and high-throughput AI workloads, ObjectScale that supports S3-over-RDMA and Nvidia CUDA libraries for large object repositories and periodic snapshots of AI models, and the Lightning File System, a fast software-defined parallel system announced at Nvidia’s GTC 2026 show in March and released a month later. It’s aimed at high-scale training and inferencing.

The platform is supported by Nvidia technology. Along with the CUDA libraries and NIM microservices, the GPU-driven platform includes Nvidia’s Nemotron Retriever models for document parsing, embedding, and reranking, and cuVS, an open source library of GPU-accelerated algorithms for vector indexing and search.

The goal is to ensure that these unified storage layers provide exabyte-scale capabilities to ensure that GPUs aren’t left waiting for data to arrive and to address what Chhabra calls the “pilot reproduction gap.”

“The use case works in the demo, or there's a small pilot rollout, and users are excited, leadership is excited,” he said. “But then when you start scaling it out, all of a sudden challenges around data governance – not having the right data, having dirty data – impacting the AI challenges or AI outcomes come in. That's really where the real enterprise scale is held back.”

Dell this week is adding more capabilities to the platform, with a focus on agentic AI. The new features are designed to give agents common context and meanings to terms that are scattered across structured and unstructured data, an easier path to finding the right context for such data, and then give them a way to use that context.

The challenge is that while agents on the platform access the same data, documents, and history, they have to reconstruct their understanding and regenerate tokens every time a query is run and more data is analyzed, Chhabra said.

“This costs extra tokens,” he said. “It often creates some churn because there's a back and forth that inevitably ends up happening with the human in the loop, which then slows things down. Often that means the answers that you're getting out of this are not fully trustworthy, so context is really what's important. What all of [the new features drive] is fewer steps and lower costs because agents don't have to keep rebuilding context in every request. They actually have data that can flow into the agent that reduces compute costs [and] the number of tokens that are generated.”

The Unified Semantic Layer provides the rules and definitions to words so they mean the same thing wherever they appear. In a use case Chhabra outlined, he noted that the word “defect” can have one definition in one manufacturing plant and another definition in a second plant. The Unified Semantic Layer, which includes a searchable glossary, lets agents understand the word means the same thing at each plant. Dell also is using Nvidia’s Auto-Ontology open source library that can create knowledge graphs from enterprise data.

The Enterprise Knowledge Graph shows how structured and unstructured data is related using metadata, lineage, and query history to continuously tune the graph. While the semantic layer can show agents what a word actually means, the knowledge graph can provide connections between that data and data in other systems.

“ If you're trying to draw some correlations between how often a defect happens and whether it's connected to a particular supplier or a particular distributor or anything in the supply chain, rather than having the model actually having to do rerun and create tokens every time, the Enterprise Knowledge Graph can actually make those connections for the model, making it much more token-efficient,” he said.

Users can then take what’s been done with the semantic layer and knowledge graph to create Knowledge Agents that each can work as a trusted agent about a particular topic. Rules can be built around them dictating the guidance it follow, how much it can spend in tokens, and what data it can see. It also uses Nvidia’s Nemotron Retriever models for reasoning and visually understanding the data.

Chhabra said Knowledge Agents also give enterprises greater flexibility in their AI environments, such as choosing the size of the AI model they’re using for a specific use case, whether to use general-purpose models in the cloud, or open source models on-premises.

Dell also is bringing Nvidia’s cuDF GPU-accelerated library to the Data Processing Engine to accelerate data processing and analytics and Apache Arrow to move data efficiently between data storage and processing so data can be queried where it sits. Organizations can now use GPUs rather than CPUs in data processing, which can mean 20 times faster batch processing of data than what can be done with a CPU, and four times the data processing speed.

The cuDF-and-Arrow combination complements the cuVS-augmented search and cuDF analytics already in the Dell Processing Engine.

With the new open source Dell Storage Performance Tool for ObjectScale and PowerScale, organizations can more accurately measure the needed size of their AI infrastructures and keep data flowing to their GPUs.

“Organizations can define the workload they want to benchmark our storage platforms with, and then checkpoints style writes, high-concurrency reads, mixed read-write environments, even high-score queries,” Chhabra said. “They can all run these benchmarks on their own infrastructure with the same tool that Dell Engineering is using internally for benchmarking our products.”

item.title: AI Spending Is The Honey Badger Of Budgets
item.description:
Trying to figure out how much money is sloshing around for AI infrastructure and services is becoming a sport. We are living through the most dramatic IT investment cycle in the history of information technology, rivaling the debut of commercial computing systems six decades ago that made IBM and several other companies fabulously wealthy (relatively speaking) at that time.

AI represents a new architecture – not so new in terms of hardware if you are a supercomputing geek, of course – and is a thing that is distinct in its own right and will be so until it becomes the dominant architecture in the datacenter. And that new architecture is growing like crazy, and the estimates for AI spending keep get revised upwards despite inflation, worries about the AI bubble bursting, power constraints, supply chain woes, political instabilities, and uncertain national and global economies. AI is the honey badger of IT budgets , and nothing is stopping forecasts revised more up as they move to the right.

And, as you may surmise, as the AI budgets are accelerating, the traditional datacenter IT spending is in recession, as it has been since 2023 when the GenAI boom took off in earnest. And it looks like traditional IT will be in recession for the foreseeable future.

This prognostication is reinforced by the latest AI spending forecasts coming out of Gartner , and specifically from John-David Lovelock , who is a distinguished vice president analyst and economist the company. As usual, I am doing to add some perspective to this forecast, and also talk about the revenue streams that support the debt that the hyperscalers, cloud builders, and AI model builders are deploying to support the $8.1 trillion investment in AI stuff from 2025 through 2027.

The contrast between AI spending and non-AI spending in the IT market is not obvious, which is why we have paired the AI forecast from Gartner with its overall IT spending forecasts. Here’s a chart that makes the traditional IT recession obvious:

If you do the math, as I did, total IT spending rose by 10.7 percent to $5.58 trillion in 2025 and is expected to rise by an even larger 14.2 percent to $6.37 trillion in 2027. Gartner has not yet provided a publicly available IT spending forecast for 2027, so I plugged in my estimate of $6.98 trillion, up 9.6 percent.

Over that time, AI spending in the aggregate rose by 2.6X in 2025 to $1.79 trillion and is anticipated to rise by 49.7 percent in 2026 to $2.67 trillion and by 36 percent to $3.64 trillion in 2027. Next year will be, if my estimate for overall IT spending is in the right ballpark, the first year where AI spending will be larger than traditional IT spending, which shrunk by 12.5 percent in 2025 to $3.79 trillion, and is expected to shrink further by 2.5 percent in 2026 to $3.69 trillion, and will shrink by 9.5 percent in 2027 to $3.43 trillion. In this interpretation of the data, I am ignoring the fact that people talk about AI smartphone or AI PCs and try to put them in the bucket. AI capabilities in these machines are largely incidental. People are buying a new phone or a new PC and it not surprisingly has features to run AI locally on these devices. That does not, in my mind, make them part of the AI infrastructure.

Here is a table that brings all the latest Gartner numbers and forecasts together in one place:

What is new with the latest forecast is that Gartner has broken licenses for GenAI models and sales of AI agents and assistants separate from sales of AI data science and machine learning platforms and more generic AI development platforms. This is distinct from the broader AI software category, which means enterprise software that has AI functionality built into it. Just like the AI PC or the AI smartphone, I am not sure if people are buying this functionality specifically, but are getting it as part of their upgrades. Many customers may be intentionally upgrading their apps to get that AI functionality, but I think it is more likely that they are upgrading capabilities even where there is not AI functionality – as is constantly happening in enterprise computing. AI is just another set of functions in the application stack, and at some point, this really is just what “software” will do.

What everyone is most keen on understanding, for the sake of the GenAI bubble expanding even more, is how AI infrastructure spending – servers, storage, and switching – is holding up. In its review of 2025, Gartner actually raised AI infrastructure spending for 2025 a bit, from $975.6 billion in its May forecast to $981.9 billion in the September forecast. For 2026, Gartner added an additional $52.9 billion, and for 2027, it added $87.4 billion. I strongly suspect this increased spending is largely due to XPUs designs created by hyperscalers and cloud builders that are being used internally and also sold to the big AI model builders like OpenAI and Anthropic. Some of it is incremental Nvidia and AMD GPU-accelerated system sales, of course.

“The buildout of AI data center capacity is the largest infrastructure project humanity has even undertaken,” Lovelock said in the statement accompanying the updated AI spending forecast. “The capacity growth from hyperscalers and service providers purchasing AI-optimized servers will continue to be the largest single area of spending.”

So just how much money will these companies generate to fuel all of this investment? Synergy Research Group provides this answer in its latest forecast of spending for cloud computing services, cloud software services, and leading consumer-oriented digital services – the companies adopting GenAI software and making infrastructure purchases to run that GenAI in production. The biggies here are Google, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, Meta Platforms, and ByteDance.

From 2026 onwards, Synergy Research’s principle analyst, John Dinsdale, is expecting for revenue growth among these service providers to grow faster than they did from 2020 through 2025. If you add up the revenues from all of these service providers for 2025, 2026, and 2027 together (and the data is a little wiggly here because we are eyeballing it from a chart, not reading a table of actual numbers), there is $6.2 trillion in revenues for IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, search, and social media searches.

Now, that revenue has to cover the costs of providing those services, which includes paying human beings salaries, health insurance, and other benefits. If you assume that 75 percent of the spending on AI stuff is done by the hyperscalers, cloud builders, and AI model builders, that works out to $6.1 trillion. The would have to spend all of their money – every penny of revenue stream – to fulfill their AI infrastructure dreams.

This is why the tech titans are turning to debt financing, vendor financing from Nvidia, AMD, and Broadcom, roundtripping deals, and other ways of getting capital to allocate to their IT spending goals. If they don’t do this, they cannot afford to invest in the future of AI at the rate they want to, which is expressed by the Gartner AI spending forecast. Neoclouds, sovereign clouds, and commercial enterprises will face the same issues to a lesser or equal degree. In all cases, AI will have to start helping to remove costs to support further AI investments.

There is no other way to do this except to keep borrowing from the future. And as that chart from Synergy Research shows for the years 2028 through 2031, the revenue streams are going to more than double. So, if this all pans out as expected, there is a big future to borrow against and that borrowing is what can make that future actually happen.

We shall see. As I have said many times, the only way to predict the future is to actually live it.

item.title: Micron’s Numbers Show Why HBM4 Memory Is Worth 15X Its Weight In Gold
item.description:
It may turn out that HBM stacked DRAM is the most profitable product in the six decade history of commercial information technology. IBM’s mainframe engines in the 1970s might be in the same zone, depending on how you allocate costs and revenues. But my gut says in terms of driving revenues and profits, HBM stacked DRAM packaging beats the monolithic systems technology (MST) packaging of the System/370s in the 1970s and the thermal conduction module (TCM) packaging of the System/3081 in the 1980s.

It just goes to show you how valuable advanced packaging has been in the past and how it still matters here in the future.

And no matter what, the growth of the HBM market, and the revenues of Micron Technology, Samsung, and SK Hynix are skyrocketing much faster than the IBM mainframe ever did. This is a thing to behold, and it underpins the growth of Nvidia and AMD. Not to put too fine a point on it, but without the high bandwidth stacked DRAM these companies make, the GenAI revolution would not – and could not – have happened.

I have been covering Micron’s financials since this boom started, and I will be adding Samsung and SK Hynix in the next round of numbers to complete the set. But for now, let’s go over the results from Micron in its fiscal 2026 ended on September 3. The numbers are downright agog.  ( Or maybe they are upright gog. . . . )

In the quarter, Micron’s revenues went skyward, up 4.8X year on year to $54.23 billion. Operating income was up nearly 12X from the year ago period, to $43.75 billion, and net income also rose by 12X to $37.7 billion. Micron is bringing 69.5 percent of revenue to the bottom line, and it is not even a little tempted to try to build its memory and flash foundries any faster than its already ambitious plan.

Micron has enough cash on hand to build about nearly four fabs, at $73.45 billion, up by 7.6X from a year ago, but it only spent $10.77 billion on capital expenses because building foundries is like having a baby. You can’t have nine women split the work up in parallel and do it within a month. You have to go from conception to birth, serially. Moreover, all of the memory makers are pretty sure that the AI bubble will hold through 2028 at the very least and probably into 2030, and none of them are in any hurry to create a bust cycle where there is a massive boom.

They’re learning, like OPEC nations with oil.

The memory business has always been plagued by boom-bust cycles, and none of the DRAM and flash vendors wants to create an oversupply situation. Not when insane demand and supply shortages are driving up prices – and profits – sky high. Even if Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix could build and ramp a foundry in a year, they might choose not to because memory prices per unit capacity just keep rising. They are all trying to do the least work for the maximum revenue and the lowest possible cost, and there has never been such a shiny golden hour in the history of IT.

The DRAM business, which includes various kinds of memory chips including low-power LPDDR that is being increasingly used in some AI server systems, high capacity server memory based on regular DRAM, and “normal” DRAM for PCs, tablets, and smartphones. The DRAM business rose by 4.4X to $39.77 billion in the quarter, and despite HBM’s best intentions with rising prices, DRAM was not Micron’s fastest growing product line. Flash non-volatile storage was, with sales up 6.2X to $14.1 billion.

If capacity were not a constraint – meaning, if Micron could drop in working foundries in a few quarters rather than several years – it would still take many years for the flash business to catch up to the DRAM business. That said, for a dollar of capex, NAND flash memory foundries are easier and cheaper to add than DRAM foundries, and given the demand, I expect for Micron to build out this business as fast as is practical. The difficulty of bringing clean room DRAM foundries online – and the higher expense – is why we expect Micron to move slower here in terms of bits shipped.

No matter what, Micron’s chief technology officer, Scott DeBoer, told Wall Street analysts that the company is two generations ahead of ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), China’s up and coming indigenous memory maker, and you can bet that it will make sure it stays two generations ahead to keep its customers from moving to Chinese memory. CXMT just went public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange in July, raising $8.6 billion. Which is a pittance compared to the kind of profits its rivals are now enjoying. But you can bet that China is dead serious about supplying its own memory and trying to sell it globally. It is only a matter of time.

But for now, Micron is rolling in it.

The Cloud Memory business unit, which is dominated by HBM memory, is not as large or as profitable as the Core Datacenter business unit, which is where regular DRAM and flash are stashed. But make no mistake. At this point, both are growing crazy fast and are incredibly profitable.

In fiscal Q4, the Cloud Memory business had sales of $16.28 billion, up 3.6X year on year and up 18.3 percent sequentially. Gross income was 83 percent of sales ($13.52 billion) and operating income was 76 percent of sales ($12.38 billion). Gross income grew by 5X and net income grew by 4.7X year on year. To say that Micron has extraordinary pricing power is a massive understatement. We would love to know how much of this growth is higher pricing for HBM and high-end DRAM and how much is increased capacity.

Mark Murphy, Micron’s chief financial officer, said on the call that DRAM bits shipped rose by a single digit percentage in Q4 and that prices increased in the “high teens percentage range.” With flash, bits shipped rose by 10 percent year on year and prices increased by 30 percent. But again, these are across all products. I think the price increases for HBM, LPDDR, and high-end DRAM for servers were higher than that average and that shipments were also a lot higher than the average. There is no other way to get the kinds of numbers the Micron datacenter business has.

The Core Datacenter business was up 11X year on year to a tad over $18 billion, a testament to how DRAM and flash are core components in AI clusters, whether they are for training, inference, or AI sandboxes executing agentic AI code and tools.

Add them together, and Micron’s datacenter revenue rose by 5.6X to $34.29 billion, which was 35.6 percent sequential growth. The company’s datacenter product operating income rose by 10.7X to $27.68 billion, and represented 81 percent of revenues for the datacenter products as a whole. Amazing.

Excepting that Micron gets revenues and profits that are even higher in its mobile, client, auto, and embedded segments, and that has helped pay for development of the datacenter stuff, I really don’t care much about these. But the data is in the table above for you to peruse.

Basically, as a best friend’s mom used to say when someone was fortunate, Micron has “sat in a tub of butter.” It can do no wrong at the moment, and is just raking in the money with a combine a half acre wide.

Micron no longer gives us data, or even just good hints, about how the HBM, high-end server DRAM, and LPDDR segments of the DRAM space are doing. But I take the data we get and what I see going on in the industry and take a stab at predicting how these key three product segments do in terms of driving sales for Micron. Take a gander:

My best guess has HBM memory driving $14.33 billion in fiscal Q4, up 7.6X year on year, with high capacity server DIMMs and LPDDR memory together driving $8.05 billion in sales, up 6.1X compared to Q4 F2025. The rest of the DRAM sold by Micron I estimate to be $17.39 billion, growing at 3.1X year on year.

Going forward in 2027, Micron is going to hike the price of its HBM memory to get its profit profile in line with regular DRAM. Sanjay Mehrotra, Micron’s chief executive officer, said on the call that Micron has "completed agreements for the vast majority of our calendar 2027 HBM bit supply with significant price increases year over year, narrowing the gross margin gap with conventional DRAM."

The HBM4 ramp, Mehrotra added, is proceeding apace and the company has a “strong roadmap for future HBM products,” calling out the work the company is doing with Nvidia for the industry’s first custom-HBM4E implementation, NVHBM, which will be adopted in next generation of GPUs and NVLink Fusion platforms from Big Green.

In general, Mehrotra said that memory and flash will be under tighter constraints in calendar 2027 and 2028 than they were in calendar 2026 – sorry, folks, move along, nothing to see here. This calendar year, Micron is growing DRAM bits shipped by the mid-20s percent range, and in calendar 2027 and 2028, it will only grow in the low 20s percent. With flash, it flips, just as we hinted at above. Flash capacity shipped in calendar 2026 was in the low 20s percent range, and in calendar 2027 and 2028, it will be in the mid-20s percent range. Again, it is easier and cheaper to expand flash manufacturing than it is to expand DRAM capacity, and expanding HBM capacity is harder and harder because increasingly taller DRAM stacks running at higher speeds have a higher chance of being a manufacturing dud.

Micron did say it would expand its capex in fiscal 2027, and that this extra spending would aim to increase DRAM output. It will have to do that as it moves into HBM4E and HBM5, which are going to burn through DRAM because of dud stacks faster than HBM4 and HBM3E did. (With higher DRAM speeds and higher stacks, the yields necessarily go down. And will keep getting worse.)

And just for fun, here is the Micron HBM market forecast from June, which was not updated in the September quarter:

Crazy, isn’t it? Micron wanted to get rich, like all companies want to, but this GenAI boom has made all the memory and flash makers richer than they ever imagined.

To secure supplies of memory and flash, Micron’s customers have shelled out $32 billion on prepayments, which is why that cash pile is so high. The company has inked 26 supplier agreements that cover around 35 percent of its revenues between now and fiscal 2030, and Mehrotra said that it will eventually have agreements that represent around half of sales. Micron has $150 billion in remaining performance obligations – what is colloquially called revenue backlog – and this only represents deals with fixed price floors and committed volumes. There are presumably customers who have deals without fixed pricing and without committed volumes, but it is hard to imagine why given this environment.

As for guidance, Micron only talked about Q1 F2027, and said sales were expected to be $61.5 billion, plus or minus $1.5 billion. That is 13 percent sequential growth, which is not huge by comparisons to other quarters. But it is huge year on year, up 4.5X compared to the $13.64 billion Micron brought in for Q1 F2025.

Which brings me to my final point: A twelve-high HBM stack probably weighs somewhere around a quarter gram and costs maybe $500 to $600, depending on the customer and the volumes. At that weight, you need about 125 stacks to get a troy ounce of HBM4. That is a cost of $62,500 to $75,000 per troy ounce. Gold is trading at $4,176 per troy ounce as this story goes to press, which makes an HBM4 stack worth 15X to 18X that of gold.

Strange new world.

item.title: SPONSORED: Build the right AI factory for your needs: partner for success
item.description:
AI ambition is easy to describe - using data and models to improve decisions, automate work, accelerate discovery, or create new services. Delivering those outcomes is harder and takes a significant amount of experience to be successful.

Training a frontier model, fine-tuning an industry model, running high-volume inference and supporting agentic AI place different demands on infrastructure, processes and people. Implementing AI may include a single-purpose turnkey configuration that will accommodate one line of business, or the business may demand a more strategic approach to capitalize on the economies of scale and create AI as a multi-tenant service, designed to accommodate the multitude of mainstream business requirements.

That is the value of an AI factory, bringing the complete AI lifecycle together so a cost-effective infrastructure can be designed around the mission, scaled with demand, secured as needed and operated as a dependable source of intelligence. The AI factory is designed to deliver the capacity, performance, utilization and business value customers expect.

From AI workload to business outcome

An AI factory is an integrated solution for data ingestion, model development, training, fine-tuning, inference, monitoring and continuous improvement. Its purpose is to turn data into intelligence repeatedly and efficiently—whether that intelligence supports a clinician, an engineer, a researcher, a public service or an enterprise application.

Achieving that goal requires more than choosing an accelerated processor. Compute must match the business model and expected workloads. Networking and data pipelines must keep accelerators supplied. Storage must support the volume and velocity of data. Software must provision resources and orchestrate jobs. Security, governance and multi-tenancy must reflect who will use the environment and what data they can access. Power and cooling must support the system’s density today and as it grows.

“Without proper architecture, governance and operational expertise, organizations can't safely leverage their data, take AI into core processes, or turn innovation into durable competitive advantage,” says Thierry Pienaar, HPE Fellow, Vice President and CTO for HPC and AI Sales. “Customers are realizing the fact that to derive value to its utmost extent they need an end-to-end infrastructure that's purpose-designed and purpose-built for AI.”

Operate the environment as one system

As the use of AI expands across an organization, the operational challenges mature. Multiple teams may need different resource profiles, application stacks, service levels and data boundaries. Platform teams need to see utilization, allocate capacity, apply policy and understand consumption without creating a separate infrastructure island for every workload.

The management of these differences make time-to-production an increasingly useful way to think about AI infrastructure: How quickly can an organization cost effectively move from investment vision to an operational environment generating useful intelligence?

Many enterprises initially try to answer that question by extending their existing IT expertise. But building a DIY production AI environment from individual components requires skill sets that many enterprise IT organizations have never needed or required at this scale.

A poorly implemented AI system may technically operate while still failing economically or operationally. GPUs can sit underutilized. Data pipelines can create bottlenecks. Cooling or power constraints can limit operation and/or expansion. Security policies can prevent sensitive data and workloads from being included. Separate less understood management systems can make AI factory infrastructure difficult to operate.

"The HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA portfolio gives enterprises a range of AI solutions co-developed with NVIDIA, backed by HPE’s engineering expertise and technical capabilities to design an AI factory around their specific needs and optimize it for performance at scale." The HPE AI Factory is designed to help operators provision and govern resources, observe infrastructure, track usage and support secure multi-tenant operations. That control helps customers align capacity with workload priorities while keeping the environment easier to manage as it grows.

Make sovereignty a design requirement
